sources.news_title: Arrest warrant issued for wife of off-duty Massachusetts police officer who was found dead in home
sources.text:
Search crews closed off several public areas as they combed for clues.
Police said Friday they issued an arrest warrant for the still at-large wife of an off-duty Worcester, Massachusetts police officer who was found dead inside a home earlier in the week.
Search crews, which included the police and U.S. Marshals service, suspended their fourth day of operations Friday evening trying to find Karen Solomon, 58, in connection with the death of her husband Worcester PD Patrolman Kurt Solomon, 57.
Worcester Police Chief Paul Saucier said at a news conference Friday that an arrest warrant on a charge of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon with serious bodily injury was issued for Karen Solomon, who he said was considered armed and dangerous.
Kurt Solomon, a 31-year police veteran and father of two, was found dead inside a home early Tuesday morning.
Karen Solomon is the founder of First HELP, a first responder suicide prevention non-profit. The group helps officers dealing with mental health situations and raises awareness for suicide prevention for first responders and their families.
Saucier would not go into more details about Kurt Solomon's death but said that the nature of his injures was a "sharp object." He added that Kurt Solomon's service weapon was not missing.
Surveillance cameras captured Karen Solomon walking on the street after the incident, according to police.
Saucier said that crews used helicopters, divers, sonar and dogs during their search of Coes Reservoir.
"We're still actively pursuing this area," he told reporters Friday.
Several public areas near the reservoir, including parks, were closed indefinitely as search crews plan to continue their operations Saturday morning, Saucier said.
Anyone who sees Karen Solomon is asked to contact Worcester Police by texting 274637 or calling (508) 799-8606.

sources.news_title: Warrant issued for Massachusetts officer's wife after his death
sources.text:
Warrant issued for Massachusetts officer's wife after his death
If you or someone you love is experiencing domestic violence or an abusive relationship, call the National Domestic Abuse Hotline at 1-800-799-SAFE (1-800-799-7233) or visit www.thehotline.org. Callers can remain anonymous.
Police have issued an arrest warrant for a Massachusetts woman who has been missing for several days after her husband, a veteran Worcester police officer, was found dead inside the home they shared.
Karen Solomon, 58, is wanted on charges of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon and assault and battery with a dangerous weapon causing serious bodily injury, Worcester Police Chief Paul Saucier said during a Friday news conference. Authorities said Solomon remains missing and should be considered armed and dangerous as the search for her enters its fifth day.
Investigators have been looking for Solomon since Tuesday, when officers responding to a call at the couple's Worcester home found Officer Kurt Solomon dead. Worcester police said doorbell camera footage captured Karen Solomon walking down a nearby street wearing a T-shirt, shorts and flip-flops just minutes after officers arrived at the home. Saucier said Kurt Solomon died after suffering injuries from a sharp object, but declined to provide additional details because of the ongoing investigation.
"We will not stop until we find her, either way, here or somewhere else," Saucier said, adding that investigators hope to bring closure for the officer's family and the Worcester Police Department.
Search remains focused on Coes Pond
Authorities continue to search the area around Coes Pond in Worcester, using dive teams, police dogs, sonar equipment, helicopters and marine units, CNN reported. The city has also closed Coes Pond parks, nearby beaches and the historic Stearns Tavern until further notice while the investigation continues.
Saucier encouraged the public to continue reporting potential sightings of Karen Solomon so investigators can determine whether they are credible.
USA TODAY reached out to the Worcester Police Department for additional comment on the investigation and the search for Karen Solomon.
Officer remembered for service to community
Kurt Solomon, 57, served 31 years with the Worcester Police Department and was an Army veteran. His obituary described him as an avid golfer, fisherman and gardener who is survived by two sons, his mother, two brothers and his dog, Merle.
"He will be remembered for his many years of service to his country and his community, his witty sense of humor, and the pleasures he found on the street he lived on his whole life," the obituary says.
Who is Karen Solomon?
Before authorities began searching for her, Karen Solomon was known for advocating for first responders' mental health. According to AP News, she co-founded First H.E.L.P., an organization that supports first responders and honors those who have died by suicide, and wrote two books about the physical and psychological experiences of emergency responders.
AP News reported that Karen and Kurt Solomon had been married and shared the Worcester home where the officer was found. Authorities have declined to discuss the status of their relationship, citing domestic violence privacy rules, AP News wrote. First H.E.L.P. expressed condolences to Kurt Solomon's family and the Worcester law enforcement community after his death while reaffirming its commitment to supporting first responders. Police continue to ask that anyone who sees Karen Solomon not approach her and instead contact law enforcement immediately.
Reporter Anthony Thompson can be reached at ajthompson@usatodayco.com, or on X @athompsonUSAT.

sources.news_title: Search for wife of slain Worcester officer enters fifth day
sources.text:
Karen Solomon search enters fifth day as investigation into officer husband’s death continues
It's been five days since the search for Karen Solomon began in Worcester, Massachusetts.
She is considered to be armed and dangerous after her off-duty police officer husband was found dead, prompting the city to close several nearby recreational areas this weekend.
"No one's going to stop until we find Karen Solomon," Worcester County District Attorney Joseph Early Jr. said at a press conference on Friday.
Watch below: Worcester PD, DA update search for Karen Solomon
Worcester officers found Worcester Police Patrolman Kurt Solomon, 57, dead at a residence on Wildwood Avenue early Tuesday morning following a "domestic incident," according to authorities.
An arrest warrant on a charge of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon with serious bodily injury was issued for Solomon on Wednesday.
She is described as having dark brown hair and brown eyes. Solomon was last seen wearing pajama shorts and a tank top.
Coes Pond Beach, Columbus Park and its boardwalk, Knights of Columbus Park, Coes Park Playground and Stearns Tavern have all been closed for the weekend as authorities continue their search for her.
Coes Pond Beach Family Day has been moved to Logan Field.
Anyone who sees Karen Solomon is asked to contact police and not approach her. Residents can send tips to Worcester police by texting 274637.
A wake for Kurt Solomon will be held on Tuesday, followed by a funeral on Wednesday.
Solomon served 31 years with the Worcester Police Department and leaves behind two adult sons.

sources.text:
WORCESTER, Mass. (AP) — An arrest warrant has been issued for a mental health advocate who remained missing Saturday, more than four days after police found the Massachusetts officer she had been married to dead in their home.
Karen Solomon, 58, was last spotted in a doorbell camera video, walking down a street in a T-shirt, shorts and flip-flops early Tuesday morning, just minutes after Worcester police officers responded to a call from the home where Kurt Solomon was found dead.
Worcester Police Chief Paul Saucier said the warrant charges Karen Solomon with assault and battery with a dangerous weapon. Saucier said Kurt Solomon, a 31-year-veteran officer, was mortally injured with a sharp object — he wouldn’t say what. Meanwhile the city of Worcester said Friday that public spaces around Coes Pond will remain closed as a search involving dive teams and police dogs continues.
“Kurt was a hell of a guy. He was an awesome police officer and an awesome person, and he’s going to be truly missed,” Saucier said. A wake will be held on Tuesday and his funeral on Wednesday, the chief said.
Karen Solomon wrote two books about the physical and psychological experiences of first responders and helped start First H.E.L.P., an organization that advocates for their mental health. The Solomons shared a home and had been married, court records indicated, but authorities declined to discuss their current relationship, citing domestic violence privacy rules.

sources.news_title: Arrest warrant issued amid search for founder of police mental health group after officer husband found dead, chief says
sources.text:
Police issued an arrest warrant for a Massachusetts woman in connection with the death of her police officer husband earlier this week.
Authorities are searching for Karen Solomon, the co-founder of a group that advocates for the mental health of police officers, after Worcester police officer Kurt Solomon was found dead at the home they owned together on Tuesday.
Worcester Police Chief Paul Saucier said at a news conference on Friday that the arrest warrant charges Karen Solomon with assault and battery with a dangerous weapon with serious bodily injury. She is considered armed and dangerous, the chief said, though Kurt Solomon’s service weapon was not missing from the home.
“Right now, we’re continuing our search,” Saucier said. “We will not stop until we find her either way, here or somewhere else.”
Saucier said Solomon’s injury involved a sharp object but declined to provide further details, citing the ongoing investigation into the officer’s death.
Dispatch recordings reveal unanswered calls and a missing SUV
Worcester dispatch recordings obtained by CNN offer details about the response to the Wildwood Avenue home where Kurt Solomon was found dead Tuesday, including reports of blood inside the house, attempts to reach a female 911 caller and a missing SUV.
Around 5:30 a.m. ET, first responders were dispatched to the home for a report of a man lying in the backyard.
An officer responding to the scene reported seeing “visible blood inside the building, inside the bathroom, in the back,” according to the recordings.
The dispatcher said the person who reported the incident was a female resident of the home. When dispatchers called back, the voicemail identified the number as belonging to Karen Solomon. Police have not publicly confirmed that Solomon placed the 911 call.
The audio then captures dispatchers saying they repeatedly called the number, but no one answered.
A dispatcher asked, “Is the caller a male or female?”
“It was a female. Her voicemail on her phone is Karen Solomon,” a second dispatcher said.
According to the dispatch audio, a gray 2023 Toyota Highlander registered to the homeowners was reported missing shortly afterward, prompting a be-on-the-lookout alert around 6:19 a.m. ET. The recordings do not say who is believed to be driving the vehicle.
The timing of the police dispatch recordings aligns with the Worcester Police Department’s public account of the initial response.
Saucier said Tuesday that officers responded to Wildwood Avenue at approximately 5:28 a.m. ET for a report of a “medical person down.”
Karen and Kurt Solomon shared a home and had been married, court records indicated, but authorities declined to discuss their current relationship, citing domestic violence privacy rules, according to The Associated Press.
Authorities have also not disclosed the contents of the 911 call or a potential motive.
“Kurt was a hell of a guy,” the chief remembered him at Friday’s news conference.
“He was an awesome police officer and an awesome person and he’s going to be truly missed,” Saucier said. “The Worcester Police Department is hurting right now and we’re hoping we can bring closure to the family.”
A father who loved fishing, golfing and tending to his vegetable garden
A father of two sons and “a dedicated gardener who took pride in his vegetable garden,” Kurt Solomon, 57, was also an Army veteran who served more than three decades in the Worcester Police Department, according to his obituary.
“He will be remembered for his many years of service to his country and his community, his witty sense of humor, and the pleasures he found on the street he lived on his whole life,” the obituary said.
The New England Benevolent Association, a law enforcement labor organization, said Kurt Solomon was “known as an incredibly dependable officer, colleague and friend.”
The officer, who often donated his extra vegetable crops to the food bank, enjoyed fishing, golfing and “simply sitting on his deck with a cup of coffee.”
Worcester Mayor Joe Petty said he would miss the officer’s “caring personality and the warm smile with which he always greeted me at City Council meetings.”
“Those small interactions spoke to the kind of person he was and will be greatly missed,” Petty wrote in a tribute on Instagram.
A wake will be held on Tuesday and Solomon’s funeral will be on Wednesday, the police chief said at the news conference.
The officer’s family is “going through a lot right now,” Saucier said, adding that it is a “very difficult situation.”
Ongoing search in recreation area
Worcester has closed several nearby recreational areas and beaches for the weekend while the search for Karen Solomon continues, the city said, and people are asked to avoid Coes Pond Parks and Stearns Tavern “until further notice.” Stearns Tavern is a historical building near Coes Park.
Authorities are using divers, dogs, sonar and other types of technologies to scour the area for Karen Solomon, Saucier said.
The search continued at Coes Reservoir on Friday with marine units, helicopters, sonar and dogs, according to CNN affiliate WCVB.
The recreational area, which WCVB says is near the Solomon home, is a main focus of the search, Saucier said.
“We’re still pursuing this until the evidence leads us elsewhere,” he said.
Police previously released doorbell camera footage of Karen Solomon walking down a street in a T-shirt, shorts and flip-flops early Tuesday morning, just minutes after officers responded to a call from the home. Tips and calls are coming in and investigators are combing through other video, Saucier said.
“No one’s going to stop until we find Karen Solomon,” Worcester County District Attorney Joseph Early Jr. said.
An organization advocating for first responders
Karen Solomon is a co-founder of an organization dedicated to supporting first responders’ mental health and honoring those who have died by suicide called First H.E.L.P., the organization said in a statement Tuesday night.
“Our first concern is for the officer who lost his life, his family, his colleagues, and the Worcester law-enforcement community,” the group said in its statement. “We extend our deepest condolences to all those affected by this tragedy.”
The organization said it remains “dedicated to reducing the stigma surrounding mental health in law enforcement and the first-responder community” and will continue to carry out its work.
An author bio on Amazon describes Karen Solomon as married to a police officer and the author of two books “giving a voice to the thousands of officers in the field who can’t or won’t speak out.”
This story has been updated with additional information.
CNN’s Amanda Jackson contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Worcester police issue arrest warrant for wife of slain officer; dispatch recordings offer insight - The Boston Globe
sources.text:
Worcester police have issued an arrest warrant for Karen Solomon, the wife of a slain off-duty police officer found dead in their home and the target of an ongoing manhunt, officials said Friday.
Kurt Solomon died from injuries caused by a “sharp object,” Worcester Police Chief Paul Saucier said at a press conference. He declined to discuss the evidence in the case further.
The arrest warrant, for assault and battery with a dangerous weapon causing serious bodily injury, was issued two days ago, Saucier said.
Ring security video released earlier shows Karen Solomon walking in flip flops near what appears to be the Westside Animal Clinic on Tuesday morning just minutes after her husband, Kurt, was found dead in their home on Wildwood Avenue.
She is considered armed and dangerous, officials said.
Kurt Solomon was a 31-year veteran of the police force, according to the New England Police Benevolent Association.
In a family tribute published on the website of a Worcester funeral home, Solomon was remembered for his wit, dedicated gardening hobbies, and love for his community on the street where he grew up and spent his whole life.
His funeral will be held on Aug. 26 at Our Lady of the Angels Church.
Police urged the public to not approach Karen Solomon if she is spotted and instead contact authorities.
Kurt Solomon’s service weapon was not missing from the family home when police executed a search warrant on Tuesday, Saucier said.
He declined to comment on whether authorities believe Karen Solomon is alive or dead as the search for her continues into its fourth day.
Karen Solomon spent years writing books and launching a nonprofit to advocate for police and first responder mental health awareness and suicide prevention.
On Friday, as the search for her continued, city officials announced that various parks around Coes Pond will be closed to the public as officials investigate.
The pond, which is part of a 20-acre recreational area on the west side of the city, is close to the Westside Animal Clinic where Solomon appeared in surveillance video that police released earlier this week.
Officials Friday declined to confirm whether that is the last known sighting of Solomon that they have uncovered.
Police have conducted dive searches at Coes Pond over the past few days and targeted their search efforts near the animal clinic on the first day of the search.
Saucier said no search areas have been ruled out at this time.
“We will not stop until we find her, either way, here or somewhere else,” Saucier said.
“We just have to keep doing what we’re doing,” Worcester District Attorney Joseph Early said.
Worcester police radio transmissions show a female resident of 217 Wildwood Ave., who was apparently Karen Solomon, called 911 around 5:30 a.m. to report a “male laid out in her backyard, unknown breathing,” according to a Broadcastify recording.
When officers arrived, they discovered a man dead and blood, but did not find anyone else inside the house.
Soon after, officers called for backup and the crime scene unit. One officer was instructed to “stay with the victim,” while another was told to “watch the door, just for evidence preservation,” according to the recording.
Meanwhile, officers were trying to call back the original caller.
“Can you keep trying that number? See if they answer,” an officer asked dispatch. “We just want to know if it’s somebody from inside 217 [Wildwood Ave.] that called, or if it’s … like a neighbor or something.”
The dispatcher, who tried numerous times, said the voicemail identified the caller as Karen Solomon, according to the radio transmissions.
Police then tracked the phone number to a location near Vermont and Forkey avenues, drawing a heavy police response to the area.
She was not found.
Police also issued an alert for area departments to look out for a car registered at the Solomons’ home. It was later determined the car was in the shop, according to Broadcastify.
“Looks like she might be on foot,” an officer said.
Bryan Hecht can be reached at bryan.hecht@globe.com. Follow him on Instagram @bhechtjournalism. Shannon Larson can be reached at shannon.larson@globe.com. Follow her @shannonlarson98.

sources.text:
Karen Solomon Wanted on Assault Charge as Worcester Manhunt Continues
WORCESTER, Mass. — Karen Solomon is now wanted on an arrest warrant for assault and battery with a dangerous weapon as authorities continue searching for her following the death of her husband, Worcester Police Officer Kurt Solomon.
Worcester police announced the new charge late Friday afternoon, marking a significant development in the search that began Tuesday.
Arrest Warrant Issued
Police said the 58-year-old Solomon is charged with assault and battery with a dangerous weapon. Authorities continue to consider her armed and dangerous and warned members of the public not to approach her.
Police have not publicly detailed the circumstances underlying the new assault charge.
Search Continues
Kurt Solomon, a 31-year veteran of the Worcester Police Department, was found dead at a Wildwood Avenue home Tuesday morning.
Karen Solomon had previously been identified as a suspect whom investigators wanted to question in connection with the case. The circumstances and cause of Kurt Solomon’s death have not been publicly disclosed.
Local, state and federal authorities have participated in the search for Solomon.
Anyone who sees her should avoid approaching her and contact authorities immediately.

sources.news_title: Cherry Picking Politics in the Face of Tragedy
sources.text:
During the early morning hours of Tuesday, Aug. 18, first responders discovered the body of Kurt Solomon, a 30-year veteran of the Worcester Police Department, at his home on Wildwood Avenue. Police continue to seek the location of his wife, Karen Solomon.
The widespread speculation about the case online won’t stop, but it should.
This is an obviously devastating time for the family and friends of the couple, the breadth of which is incomprehensible to those of us who haven’t experienced it.
Many at the Worcester Police Department are also hurting. Most of us have experienced the pain of losing a long-time friend or colleague. Few of us will ever experience the unimaginable toll of being assigned to an investigation into the death of a friend or colleague.
It’s a tragedy all around. No one would argue with that.
One would expect politics to take a backseat, especially on the day the tragic death occurred. Not in the Worcester City Council.
When Cherry-Picking is Good
The Worcester City Council is on its “summer schedule,” where over a nine-week period, from July 7 to September 1, it meets just twice.
During its last meeting on July 21, the report submitted to the city council by City Manager Eric Batista’s administration recommending that the city not establish a civilian review board appeared on the agenda. Councilor Khrystian King held the report, which brought it back to the agenda on Tuesday, Aug. 18.
The Worcester Police Department reportedly received the report that led to the discovery of Officer Solomon’s body at around 5:30 AM. The case became the top local news story throughout the morning. The Worcester County District Attorney’s office held a news conference, with it broadcast on its Facebook page. That live stream began at 3:21 PM. Mayor Joe Petty appeared at that press conference.
At 4 PM, Mayor Joe Petty’s Facebook and other social media pages released the following statement:
“At the beginning of tonight’s City Council meeting, I intend to make a motion to hold Item 23f regarding a Civilian Review Board. In light of the unfortunate circumstances that occurred today involving the Worcester Police Department, I believe this is the appropriate and respectful course of action. I respectfully ask that there be no public participation on this item tonight. This important discussion should take place at a time when it can receive the full attention and consideration it deserves.”
The first reason this is objectionable: cherry-picking one item to hold out of “respect” and calling it the “appropriate” thing to do paints police oversight as offensive. The foundation of the American government, three co-equal branches, is in itself oversight. To find oversight offensive is to find the United States Constitution offensive. Rescheduling the meeting in its entirety would have been the far more appropriate action.
The second reason this is objectionable is far more insidious.
The city council meeting on Tuesday started at 6 PM, as the council schedules its summer meetings half an hour earlier than most meetings for no discernible reason. Despite this being the biggest news story of the day, and Petty being at the news conference 40 minutes earlier, this announcement came just two hours before a meeting that advocates for a civilian review board organized over the last four weeks.
This was an obvious trap. Paint hearing the item on police oversight as disrespectful and inappropriate in a public notice issued with as little lead time as possible, then sit back and wait for someone to come in and say something that can be used to paint all advocates with a smear.
The tactic failed spectacularly. Just a few speakers appeared for public comment after rapid organizing by a coalition group advocating for civilian review.
A councilor raised a motion to suspend the meeting soon afterward. The council’s response defies decency.
When Cherry-Picking is Bad
See the motion by City Council Vice Chair and Councilor At-Large Khrystian King and the response from City Councilor At-Large Moe Bergman, running 2:33 combined.
King’s motion was entirely appropriate. Enabling the council to vote only on items required for city operations, like its financial matters, which are typically approved without discussion, is a reasonable response to the circumstances.
Bergman’s question of whether or not a city agency requested the meeting cancelled is just plain odd. Doing the decent thing doesn’t require the permission of a city agency.
Similarly, Bergman’s concern about council orders, which are almost always non-binding with no force of law, is strange. If there were individual items of importance, there was a willingness to enable those items to be taken up before adjourning.
No councilor proposed the idea of coming to work any time before its next meeting on Sept. 8. Coming to work only appears to be a theme when politically convenient.
King’s motion to postpone the meeting required eight votes to pass. It failed, with Councilor John Fresolo and the nexus of the anti-oversight wing, Councilors Berman, Jose Rivera, and Kate Toomey opposed. When King asked for reconsideration on the item later in the meeting, the same four voted against it again.
The council observed no moment of silence for Kurt Solomon, nor was the tragedy referred to by anyone but King. It refused to adjourn after only the necessary items on its agenda out of respect for those involved. It refused to exhibit common decency.
But oversight? Well, that’s just offensive.
Image courtesy of City of Worcester
